newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish wheat import plan seen put on hold.
newsitem.headline: Turkish wheat import plan seen put on hold.

text.p: Turkey may delay its wheat import intention because local wheat prices have begun falling after recent wheat sales in the local market by the grain board (TMO), officials and traders said on Monday.

"The import plan will be implemented if there is a need for it. The TMO has the right to import up to 500,000 tonnes and it will resort to this when needed," said a senior agriculture ministry official, who declined to be named.
"The TMO has begun selling wheat in the local market and this is envisaged to meet the local demand for some time," he told Reuters. He did not say how much the TMO has sold.

Agriculture Minister Musa Demirci reiterated last week the plan by the TMO, which holds about 700,000 tonnes of milling wheat in its stocks, that it might import up to 500,000 tonnes to stop rising wheat and bread prices.
Its import intention caused wheat prices to surge in international commodity markets.
But Turkish officials have failed to announce a firm date to tender to buy the required wheat.

A further statement by agriculture officials last week that the government was planning a decree to cut a 15-percent wheat import tax, imposed in September to limit imports after a better harvest this year, has also contributed to speculation that Turkey will import fairly soon.
The agricultural official abstained to comment on the status of the decree, which would enable the TMO, private traders and millers to import at cheaper prices.
"Importers are already importing at prices way below the local wheat prices," he said.
Turkey said on Thursday it would decrease bread prices on a nationwide basis by about 15 percent to a fixed price of 15,000 lira per loaf.
Traders said November was unfavourable for Turkey to import wheat and a possible decrease in international prices next month would be more viable for Turkey.
"Prices may later fall. We feel the government has suspended its import plan and will delay the (tax reduction) decree for a certain period," said a trader from a Western trade company.

Turkey has been considering wheat imports after bread and wheat prices rose by about 30 percent locally following a clampdown on wheat imports from the United States on grounds they might contain ergot fungus.
The United States then suspended issuing health certificates for exports to Turkey, virtually banning sales of wheat and several other grains to Turkey.
Turkey later eased the zero-tolerance requirement to 0.05 percent for ergot fungus -- a level seen as the world standard for the fungus.
But this was not found satisfactory by the United States, which last week said Turkey was now applying the zero-tolerance policy for other disease types.
